pos: adj. (of the colour of gold; in the law a diagnostic sign of leprosy in the hair, and in the Psalms the colour of a redeemed people's wings)
etymology: Old English geolu, akin to gold and to Latin helvus, pale yellow. The Hebrew tsahob is the sallow yellow of diseased hair; charuts in Psalm 68 is the yellow of refined gold.
biblical_def: The word runs at both ends of the scale. In Leviticus 13 it is a symptom the priest is trained to look for: “if it be in sight deeper than the skin; and there be in it a yellow thin hair; then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is a dry scall, even a leprosy upon the head or beard” (Lev 13:30). The examination is patient and exact — if after seven days “the scall spread not, and there be in it no yellow hair” (Lev 13:32), the man is not condemned; but if the scall has spread, “the priest shall not seek for yellow hair; he is unclean” (Lev 13:36), because spreading has already settled the case. Then Psalm 68 takes the same colour for glory: “Though ye have lien among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold” (Psa 68:13). A people blackened in the ash of the kitchen — slaves in Egypt, sleeping among the pots — are to shine like a dove in the sun. Between the two lies the whole gospel: the same eye that examines the sallow hair covers the redeemed with gold.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines yellow as being of a bright saffron color, or of the colour of gold; and notes it among the primary colours of the rainbow.
webster_full: YELLOW, a. Being of a bright saffron color, or of a color partaking of that of gold.
There be in it a yellow thin hair. Lev. xiii.
YELLOW, n. A bright color, reflecting more light than any other except white.
YELLOWNESS, n. The quality of being yellow.
scriptures: Then the priest shall see the plague: and, behold, if it be in sight deeper than the skin; and there be in it a yellow thin hair; then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is a dry scall, even a leprosy upon the head or beard.
And in the seventh day the priest shall look on the plague: and, behold, if the scall spread not, and there be in it no yellow hair, and the scall be not in sight deeper than the skin;
Then the priest shall look on him: and, behold, if the scall be spread in the skin, the priest shall not seek for yellow hair; he is unclean.
Though ye have lien among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold.
corruption_summary: Leviticus 13 is dismissed as primitive medicine, though its whole procedure is a lesson in patient, evidenced judgment rather than in hygiene.
corruption_paragraphs: The leprosy chapters are the standard example given when the law is called a relic of ancient superstition, and the charge misses what the chapter is doing. The priest is not a physician prescribing a cure; he is an appointed examiner rendering a verdict about a man's standing in the congregation. And the procedure is remarkable for its restraint. He looks; if the evidence is ambiguous he shuts the man up seven days and looks again; if there is no spreading and no yellow hair, the man is pronounced clean and washes his clothes. Only a spreading plague settles the matter. The whole apparatus is a rebuke to hasty judgment in the church — a verdict rendered on stated evidence, after a set interval, by a man under authority, with an explicit provision for finding the accused clean.

The other half of the word supplies the mercy the chapter cannot. The leper of Leviticus 13:45 goes with rent clothes and covered lip crying Unclean, unclean, and there is nothing in the law that makes him otherwise. Psalm 68 sings of a people who lay among the pots — the phrase suggests the sooty ash by a kitchen fire, or the brick-kilns of Egypt — and says they shall be as a dove's wings covered with silver and her feathers with yellow gold. The transformation is entirely one-sided. The dove does not scrub herself into brightness; she is covered. Where the modern corruption speaks of self-improvement and the recovery of one's own dignity, Scripture speaks of a covering given to those who had none, and the New Testament names it: the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsahob (H6669), yellow, of diseased hair; charuts (H2742), sharpened, hence refined gold, in Psalm 68:13; netheq (H5424), the scall of Leviticus 13.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsahob (H6669) — yellow, golden-sallow; used only of the hair in the scall; Leviticus 13:30, Leviticus 13:32.
Hebrew netheq (H5424) — a scall, a scab of the head or beard; the specific plague examined; Leviticus 13:30.
Hebrew charuts (H2742) — gold, from a root meaning sharpened or refined; her feathers with yellow gold; Psalm 68:13.
Hebrew tame (H2931) — unclean; the priest's verdict, and the cry of the leper himself; Leviticus 13:45.
Hebrew yownah (H3123) — a dove; the figure of the covered and shining people; Psalm 68:13.
usage: “A yellow thin hair… the priest shall pronounce him unclean” — a verdict on stated evidence.
“The priest shall not seek for yellow hair” — spreading has already settled it.
“Her feathers with yellow gold” — a people out of the ash pits, covered.

pos: adj. (dusky; in the Authorized Version the colour of the sheep Jacob took for his hire from Laban)
etymology: Old English brun, dark, dusky. The Hebrew chum means scorched or dark, and it appears only in the Jacob and Laban account, where the colour of a beast decided a man's wages.
biblical_def: Every occurrence of this word is in one chapter of Genesis, and the whole chapter turns on a bargain about colour. Jacob names his own wages: “I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire” (Gen 30:32). Ordinary Near Eastern sheep were white and goats were dark, so Jacob asked for the exceptions — the least likely animals, which is why Laban agreed at once. Laban then removed those very animals: “he removed that day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted… and all the brown among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons” (Gen 30:35), putting three days' journey between them and Jacob. Jacob worked with what was left: “And Jacob did separate the lambs, and set the faces of the flocks toward the ringstraked, and all the brown in the flock of Laban” (Gen 30:40). The increase came, and Jacob's own summary in the next chapter gives the true account of it: “Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me” (Gen 31:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines brown as a dusky color, inclining to redness; and notes it as compounded of black and red, or of black, red and yellow.
webster_full: BROWN, a. Dusky; of a dark or dusky color, inclining to redness.
All the brown cattle among the sheep. Gen. xxx.
BROWN, n. A dark dusky color inclining to redness.
BROWNNESS, n. A brown color.
scriptures: I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire.

And he removed that day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted, and all the she goats that were speckled and spotted, and every one that had some white in it, and all the brown among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons.

And Jacob did separate the lambs, and set the faces of the flocks toward the ringstraked, and all the brown in the flock of Laban; and he put his own flocks by themselves, and put them not unto Laban's cattle.
Gen 31:9
Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me.
corruption_summary: Jacob's prosperity is credited either to his cleverness with rods or to folk superstition, while Jacob himself and the angel in the next chapter credit it to God.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 30 is one of the passages most often used to prove that the patriarchal narratives preserve primitive folk belief — peeled rods set in the watering troughs so that the flocks would conceive striped young. The text is more careful than its critics. It reports what Jacob did without ever saying that the rods produced the result, and Genesis 31 supplies the explanation from two sources: the angel of God in a dream, who told Jacob what he had seen of Laban's dealings, and Jacob's own confession that God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me. The narrative allows Jacob his scheming, records it without approval, and then removes the credit from it entirely. That is the pattern of the whole Jacob story, in which a man contrives at every turn and is prospered in spite of his contrivances.

Laban is the other lesson and he is the more common figure. He agreed to the wage, then went the same day and removed every animal that would have paid it, and set three days between Jacob and the flock. Genesis says he changed Jacob's wages ten times. This is the ordinary conduct of an employer who has power and no fear of God, and Scripture is not neutral about it: the law commands that the hired man's wage not stay overnight, and James says the hire of the labourers kept back by fraud crieth, and the cries are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth. The brown sheep are a small detail in a long account, and what they mark is a bargain honestly made and dishonestly kept — with the outcome, in the end, entirely out of the dishonest man's hands.
roots_summary: Hebrew chum (H2345), dark, dusky, brown — found only in Genesis 30; with naqod (H5348), speckled, and talu (H2921), spotted, the other terms of the bargain.
roots_lines: Hebrew chum (H2345) — scorched, dark brown; used only of Laban's sheep; Genesis 30:32, Genesis 30:40.
Hebrew naqod (H5348) — speckled; the goats of the same bargain; Genesis 30:32.
Hebrew aqod (H6124) — ringstraked, banded at the ankles; Genesis 30:35.
Hebrew sakar (H7939) — hire, wages; of such shall be my hire; Genesis 30:32.
Hebrew natsal (H5337) — to strip away, to deliver; God hath taken away the cattle of your father; Genesis 31:9.
usage: “All the brown cattle among the sheep… of such shall be my hire” — a wage set in the unlikely animals.
“He removed that day… all the brown among the sheep” — the bargain kept in word and broken in fact.
“God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me” — the credit removed from the rods.

pos: adj. (somewhat red; in the law a mark to be examined in skin, in a garment, and in the wall of a house)
etymology: English red with the diminutive -ish. The Hebrew adamdam is a reduplicated form of adom, red — the grammar itself means reddish, a shade rather than the colour.
biblical_def: The word belongs entirely to the priest's examination, and its precision is the point. In a scar: “And in the place of the boil there be a white rising, or a bright spot, white, and somewhat reddish, and it be shewed to the priest” (Lev 13:19). In a bald head: “And if there be in the bald head, or bald forehead, a white reddish sore; it is a leprosy sprung up in his bald head” (Lev 13:42), and the priest looks again to confirm it (Lev 13:43). In cloth: “And if the plague be greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; it is a plague of leprosy, and shall be shewed unto the priest” (Lev 13:49). And in masonry: “if the plague be in the walls of the house with hollow strakes, greenish or reddish, which in sight are lower than the wall” (Lev 14:37). The same corruption is traced from a man's body into his clothing and then into his house. Uncleanness in Scripture does not stay where it started.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reddish as somewhat red; moderately red; and reddishness as the quality of being moderately red.
webster_full: REDDISH, a. Somewhat red; moderately red.
A white rising, or a bright spot, white, and somewhat reddish. Lev. xiii.
REDDISHNESS, n. Redness in a moderate degree.
RED, a. Of a bright color, resembling blood.
scriptures: And in the place of the boil there be a white rising, or a bright spot, white, and somewhat reddish, and it be shewed to the priest;
And if there be in the bald head, or bald forehead, a white reddish sore; it is a leprosy sprung up in his bald head, or his bald forehead.
And if the plague be greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; it is a plague of leprosy, and shall be shewed unto the priest:
And he shall look on the plague, and, behold, if the plague be in the walls of the house with hollow strakes, greenish or reddish, which in sight are lower than the wall;
corruption_summary: The law's attention to a faint shade is mocked as fussiness, though the same procedure follows the plague from a man's skin into his clothes and his walls.
corruption_paragraphs: It is easy to be amused by a code that legislates about a spot which is somewhat reddish. But the sequence in Leviticus 13 and 14 is the argument, and it is not funny. What begins in a man's skin appears next in his garment, in the warp and the woof, and then in the walls of the house he lives in. Stone by stone the infected building is scraped and, if the plague returns, pulled down. Whatever the exact medical identification, the doctrine encoded is unmistakable: defilement spreads outward from a person into what he wears and where he dwells. The New Testament reasons in exactly this way about sin in a congregation — a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump — and about a man's own members, which are to be mortified rather than managed.

The second corruption is subtler and it runs in the other direction. Because the shades are so carefully specified, some readers conclude that God is chiefly concerned with technical exactness — and either recoil from Him as a pedant or take up the same spirit toward their brethren. The chapters themselves refuse both. The priest is required to look, to wait, to look again, and to pronounce clean wherever the evidence permits; the standard for condemnation is a spreading plague, and the standard for acquittal is generous. The Lord Jesus met an actual leper, put forth His hand and touched him, and said, I will; be thou clean — and the man was cleansed rather than the Lord defiled. That is the reversal the whole apparatus was pointing to, and it is why a Christian reads these chapters with sober attention rather than embarrassment.
roots_summary: Hebrew adamdam (H125), reddish, a reduplication of adom (H122), red; with nega (H5061), a plague or stroke, the standing word for what is examined.
roots_lines: Hebrew adamdam (H125) — reddish, somewhat red; used of skin, garment and wall; Leviticus 13:19, Leviticus 14:37.
Hebrew yeraqraq (H3422) — greenish, the companion shade in the same clauses; Leviticus 13:49.
Hebrew nega (H5061) — a stroke, a plague; the word for whatever the priest examines; Leviticus 13:2.
Hebrew tsaraath (H6883) — leprosy, the defiling disease of skin, cloth and house; Leviticus 13:2, Leviticus 14:34.
Hebrew adom (H122) — red; the root, and the colour of Esau's pottage and of Adam's dust; Genesis 25:30.
usage: “A bright spot, white, and somewhat reddish” — a shade, examined by an appointed man.
“Greenish or reddish in the garment” — the plague following a man into his clothes.
“In the walls of the house” — and then into where he lives.

pos: adj. (somewhat green; with reddish, the two colours of the plague in a garment or a wall)
etymology: English green, Old English grene, with -ish. The Hebrew yeraqraq is again a reduplicated form — a faint or streaky green, the colour of mould and verdigris.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice, and both times it is paired with reddish and both times the subject is not a person but a possession. In cloth: “And if the plague be greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; it is a plague of leprosy, and shall be shewed unto the priest” (Lev 13:49). In a house: “And he shall look on the plague, and, behold, if the plague be in the walls of the house with hollow strakes, greenish or reddish, which in sight are lower than the wall” (Lev 14:37). The detail lower than the wall means the discolouration has eaten below the surface — it is not a stain but a depth. The remedy is graduated: the affected stones are taken out and carried to an unclean place outside the city, the house is scraped within, the dust carried out, new stones and new morter brought in; and if the plague comes again, “he shall break down the house, the stones of it, and the timber thereof, and all the morter of the house” (Lev 14:45). Nothing is painted over.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines greenish as somewhat green; having a tinge of green; and green as the colour of growing plants, or that of the spectrum between blue and yellow.
webster_full: GREENISH, a. Somewhat green; having a tinge of green.
If the plague be greenish or reddish in the garment. Lev. xiii.
GREEN, a. Of the color of herbage and plants when growing.
GREENNESS, n. The quality of being green; viridity.
scriptures: And if the plague be greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; it is a plague of leprosy, and shall be shewed unto the priest:
And he shall look on the plague, and, behold, if the plague be in the walls of the house with hollow strakes, greenish or reddish, which in sight are lower than the wall;
And he shall break down the house, the stones of it, and the timber thereof, and all the morter of the house; and he shall carry them forth out of the city into an unclean place.
Lev 13:2

When a man shall have in the skin of his flesh a rising, a scab, or bright spot, and it be in the skin of his flesh like the plague of leprosy; then he shall be brought unto Aaron the priest, or unto one of his sons the priests:
corruption_summary: A house is thought to be merely property, while Leviticus 14 treats a dwelling as a thing that can be defiled and must be dealt with, not merely redecorated.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the places a man lives are not morally inert. Leviticus 14 takes a plague in a wall as seriously as a plague in a body, and prescribes the same sequence: examination, an interval, a graduated remedy, and demolition if the corruption returns. A Christian household is not sanctified by its address, but what is kept in a house, what is watched in it, what is spoken in it and what is tolerated in it will work into the timbers of a family's life. The word lower than the wall is the whole warning. What is only on the surface can be washed; what has eaten below it must be taken out stone by stone, and the stones must go outside the city.

The other thing this small word teaches is how thorough a real remedy is. The priest does not scrape the wall and hope. He removes the affected stones, has the whole house scraped within round about, has the dust carried outside, and requires other stones and other morter to be brought and the house replastered; and if the plague breaks out again after all that, the house comes down entire and its rubble is carried away. Applied to sin, this is the difference between resolving to do better and actually removing the occasions — the account closed, the friendship ended, the device given up, the arrangement dissolved. The Lord Jesus used the same severity of figure with the right eye and the right hand. And the promise attached to the whole chapter is that the house may be pronounced clean, which is why the procedure exists at all: it is a law aimed at restoration, not at condemnation.
roots_summary: Hebrew yeraqraq (H3422), greenish, from yaraq, to be green; with shaqaarurah, hollow strakes, and nathats (H5422), to break down.
roots_lines: Hebrew yeraqraq (H3422) — greenish, faintly green; used of a garment and of a wall; Leviticus 13:49, Leviticus 14:37.
Hebrew yaraq (H3418) — green herbs, greenness; the root of the colour.
Hebrew shethi (H8359) and erev (H6154) — the warp and the woof, the lengthwise and crosswise threads of the cloth; Leviticus 13:49.
Hebrew nathats (H5422) — to pull down, to break down; he shall break down the house; Leviticus 14:45.
Hebrew taher (H2891) — to be clean, to pronounce clean; the verdict the whole procedure is aimed at; Leviticus 14:48.
usage: “Greenish or reddish in the garment… in the warp, or in the woof” — examined thread by thread.
“Which in sight are lower than the wall” — not a stain but a depth.
“He shall break down the house” — when the remedy has been tried and the plague returns.

pos: adj. (flashing, glittering; the Authorized Version's word for the Lord's raiment on the mount of transfiguration)
etymology: Middle English glisteren, to shine or sparkle, akin to glisten. The Greek exastrapto is stronger — to flash out like lightning — and it is used only here in the New Testament.
biblical_def: One occurrence, and it is on a mountain: “And as he prayed, the fashion of his countenance was altered, and his raiment was white and glistering” (Luk 9:29). Matthew has “his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light” (Mat 17:2). The three synoptic accounts agree that the change came while He was praying, that Moses and Elijah appeared with Him, and that the Father's voice named Him the beloved Son. Two things distinguish this shining from every other in Scripture. Moses' face shone after he had been with God, and he did not know it (Exo 34:29) — a reflected glory, borrowed and fading. Here the light comes from within: the fashion of His countenance was altered, and the garments took the light rather than giving it. Peter, who was there, appeals to it as evidence rather than as vision: “For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2Pe 1:16). And John sees the same countenance in Patmos, “as the sun shineth in his strength” (Rev 1:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to glister as to shine, to be bright, to sparkle, to be brilliant; glistering is its participle, used of a flashing brightness.
webster_full: GLISTER, v.i. To shine; to be bright; to sparkle; to be brilliant.
All that glisters is not gold.
GLISTERING, ppr. Shining; sparkling; splendid.
His raiment was white and glistering. Luke ix.
scriptures: Luk 9:29
And as he prayed, the fashion of his countenance was altered, and his raiment was white and glistering.
Mat 17:2
And was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light.
For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.

And it came to pass, when Moses came down from mount Sinai with the two tables of testimony in Moses' hand, when he came down from the mount, that Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone while he talked with him.
corruption_summary: The transfiguration is reduced to a symbolic vision or an inner experience of the disciples, though Peter cites it as eyewitness evidence against cunningly devised fables.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern critical treatment of Luke 9 offers two exits from the plain sense: the scene is a resurrection appearance moved backward into the ministry, or it is a symbolic composition expressing the church's faith. Second Peter closes both. Writing to churches under pressure, Peter says the apostles did not follow cunningly devised fables; they were eyewitnesses of His majesty; they heard the voice from the excellent glory when they were with Him in the holy mount. He offers the event as testimony to a fact, in exactly the register a man uses when he expects to be believed about something that happened. And he then makes a striking comparison: we have also a more sure word of prophecy. Having seen the glory with his own eyes, Peter directs the churches to the written word as the surer ground, which is a rebuke to every claim that experience outranks Scripture.

The comparison with Moses is the doctrinal heart of the word. In Exodus the skin of Moses' face shone because he had talked with God, and he did not know it, and Paul says the shining was fading, so that the veil hid the end of that which is abolished. On the mount of transfiguration the light is not caught from outside; the fashion of the countenance is altered and the raiment flashes with it. The disciples were seeing, for a moment, what had been veiled by the flesh all along — the glory of the only begotten of the Father, who had emptied Himself of no divinity but had hidden it. And Moses himself is standing there, talking with Him of the decease He should accomplish at Jerusalem. The glory is real, and it walks down the mountain toward a cross.
roots_summary: Greek exastrapto (G1823), to flash forth as lightning, used only at Luke 9:29; with metamorphoo (G3339), to be transfigured, and doxa (G1391), glory.
roots_lines: Greek exastrapto (G1823) — to flash out like lightning; his raiment was white and glistering; Luke 9:29.
Greek metamorphoo (G3339) — to be changed in form; used of Christ on the mount and of the believer's renewed mind; Matthew 17:2, Romans 12:2.
Greek doxa (G1391) — glory; they saw his glory, and the two men that stood with him; Luke 9:32.
Greek epoptes (G2030) — an eyewitness, one admitted to a sight; eyewitnesses of his majesty; 2 Peter 1:16.
Hebrew qaran (H7160) — to send out rays, to shine; the skin of Moses' face shone; Exodus 34:29.
usage: “As he prayed, the fashion of his countenance was altered” — the change came in prayer.
“Eyewitnesses of his majesty” — offered as testimony, not as symbol.
“Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone” — a borrowed light, and a fading one.

pos: adj. (even, free from roughness; used of Jacob's neck, of David's stones, and of the preaching a rebellious people demand)
etymology: Old English smoth. The Hebrew chalaq means smooth or slippery, and the same root gives both the smooth stones of the brook and the smooth things false prophets are asked to speak.
biblical_def: Four uses, and they are a sermon in themselves. Deception: “And Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man” (Gen 27:11); so his mother “put the skins of the kids of the goats upon his hands, and upon the smooth of his neck” (Gen 27:16), and Isaac said, The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau (Gen 27:22). Faith: “And he took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook… and his sling was in his hand: and he drew near to the Philistine” (1Sa 17:40) — stones made smooth by water, chosen by a shepherd, against a champion in brass. Idolatry: “Among the smooth stones of the stream is thy portion; they, they are thy lot” (Isa 57:6). And the corruption of preaching: “Which say to the seers, See not; and to the prophets, Prophesy not unto us right things, speak unto us smooth things, prophesy deceits” (Isa 30:10). Isaiah names them in the previous verse for what they are — “a rebellious people, lying children, children that will not hear the law of the LORD” (Isa 30:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines smooth as having an even surface, free from roughness or asperities; and figuratively, bland, mild, soothing, flattering in speech.
webster_full: SMOOTH, a. Having an even surface, or a surface so even that no roughness or points are perceptible to the touch.
2. Evenly spread; glossy; as a smooth stone.
3. Bland; mild; soothing; flattering. Speak unto us smooth things. Isa. xxx.
4. Gently flowing; moving equably; as smooth waters.
scriptures: Which say to the seers, See not; and to the prophets, Prophesy not unto us right things, speak unto us smooth things, prophesy deceits:
Isa 30:9
That this is a rebellious people, lying children, children that will not hear the law of the LORD:

And he took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd's bag which he had, even in a scrip; and his sling was in his hand: and he drew near to the Philistine.
And Jacob went near unto Isaac his father; and he felt him, and said, The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 30:10 puts the demand for smooth preaching in the mouth of the congregation, which is where our own age is least willing to look for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is usually cited against false prophets, and it does condemn them; but the sentence Isaiah records is spoken by the people. They say to the seers, See not; to the prophets, Prophesy not unto us right things; speak unto us smooth things. The supply follows the demand. That is the uncomfortable half of the doctrine, and Paul says the same thing in plainer language: the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears. Note the direction of the verb — they heap teachers to themselves. A congregation that has decided what it will not hear will find someone to not say it, and in an age of unlimited choice in preaching the sorting happens quietly and completely. The remedy is not chiefly to denounce the smooth speakers but for hearers to ask what they have made it impossible for a faithful man to say to them.

The other uses guard the word from becoming a mere slogan for severity. David chose smooth stones, and their smoothness was not a fault; it was the brook's long work, and it made them fly true. There is a smoothness that is polish and a smoothness that is deceit, and Scripture distinguishes them by what they are for. Jacob's smooth neck under goatskins is deceit; the flatterer's words are smoother than butter while war is in his heart. But a well-made sentence, a gentle answer, a preacher who has laboured until the truth is clear and unstumbling — that is smoothness in the service of truth, and the Bible itself is full of it. The test is Isaiah's: does the smoothness carry right things, or was it purchased by leaving them out?
roots_summary: Hebrew chalaq (H2509), smooth, slippery, flattering — the root of both the smooth stones and the smooth words; with chalaqlaqqah, slippery places.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalaq (H2509) — smooth; I am a smooth man, and the smooth stones of the brook; Genesis 27:11, 1 Samuel 17:40.
Hebrew chalaqqah — smooth things, flatteries; speak unto us smooth things; Isaiah 30:10.
Hebrew marah (H4784) — to be rebellious; the character of the people who demand them; Isaiah 30:9.
Hebrew nachal (H5158) — a brook, a torrent bed; where the five stones were made smooth; 1 Samuel 17:40.
Greek knetho (G2833) — to itch; having itching ears, they heap up teachers; 2 Timothy 4:3.
usage: “Speak unto us smooth things, prophesy deceits” — and it is the people who say it.
“Chose him five smooth stones out of the brook” — smoothness made by long water, and it flew true.
“The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau” — smoothness under goatskins.

pos: adj. and adv. (level, without rising; used of a disqualifying blemish in a priest and of a prophet falling flat before the angel of the LORD)
etymology: Old Norse flatr, level. The Authorized Version uses it twice: once of a nose in the list of blemishes, and once adverbially of a man's whole body on the ground.
biblical_def: The law lists the blemishes that barred a son of Aaron from approaching the altar: “For whatsoever man he be that hath a blemish, he shall not approach: a blind man, or a lame, or he that hath a flat nose, or any thing superfluous” (Lev 21:18). He was not cast out — the same chapter says he shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy — but he might not go in unto the veil nor come nigh unto the altar. The priesthood had to be visibly whole because it pointed to a Priest who is. The other use is Balaam: “Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand: and he bowed down his head, and fell flat on his face” (Num 22:31). A man who had been arguing with a beast and who intended to sell his prophesying went down full length in the road, and it took an opened eye to do it. The word in both places marks the difference between what a man may do at the altar and what he must do before God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines flat as having an even surface, without risings or indentures; level; also lying prostrate at length upon the ground.
webster_full: FLAT, a. Having an even surface, without risings or indentures, hills or valleys.
2. Level with the ground; fallen; laid low; as, the wall lies flat.
3. Prostrate; lying the whole length on the ground. He fell flat on his face. Num. xxii.
4. Insipid; dead; vapid; as flat drink.
scriptures: For whatsoever man he be that hath a blemish, he shall not approach: a blind man, or a lame, or he that hath a flat nose, or any thing superfluous,
Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand: and he bowed down his head, and fell flat on his face.
Heb 4:15
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
corruption_summary: Leviticus 21 is read as contempt for the disabled, when the chapter provides for the blemished priest's food and honour and bars only his approach to the altar, for a reason about Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The list of blemishes is one of the passages most often produced as evidence that the God of the Old Testament despised the weak, and the chapter itself refutes the charge in the verses that follow. The blemished priest shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy; he keeps his family, his tribe, his portion and his standing among the priests. What is withheld is the act of going in unto the veil and coming nigh unto the altar. The restriction is not a judgment on his worth but a requirement of the sign: the man who represented Israel before God had to be outwardly unmarred because he stood for a Priest who is inwardly and outwardly without flaw. Hebrews says it plainly — such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners — and adds that He is nonetheless touched with the feeling of our infirmities.

It is worth setting 1 Samuel 16:7 beside this, because the two verses are sometimes played against each other. God tells Samuel that man looketh on the outward appearance but the LORD looketh on the heart — and God is the one who gave the law about the flat nose. There is no contradiction. The priestly requirement was about a type, a visible sign given to a people who were being taught by signs; the choice of David was about a king's heart, and God passed over the tall brother. The two together forbid both errors: the church may not treat physical appearance as a measure of spiritual worth, and it may not pretend that the outward forms God appointed were arbitrary. Balaam is the closing comment. A man with no blemish at all in his body, and a full commercial interest in his prophesying, ended flat in the road because his eyes were opened.
roots_summary: Hebrew charum (H2763), flat or mutilated, of the nose; mum (H3971), a blemish; with shachah (H7812), to bow down, and qadad (H6915), to bow the head, of Balaam.
roots_lines: Hebrew charum (H2763) — flat, slit, mutilated; he that hath a flat nose; Leviticus 21:18.
Hebrew mum (H3971) — a blemish, a spot; whatsoever man hath a blemish shall not approach; Leviticus 21:18, Leviticus 22:20.
Hebrew qadad (H6915) — to bow the head; he bowed down his head; Numbers 22:31.
Hebrew shachah (H7812) — to prostrate oneself, to worship; the whole-body posture of Numbers 22:31.
Greek amomos (G299) — without blemish; Christ offered himself without spot to God, and the church is to be presented so; Hebrews 9:14, Ephesians 5:27.
usage: “He that hath a flat nose… shall not approach” — and he still eats the bread of his God.
“Fell flat on his face” — a hired prophet, when his eyes were opened.
“Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” — from the same God who gave the law.

pos: adj. (slender, meagre; the word of Pharaoh's dream for the ears and kine that devoured the full ones)
etymology: Old English thynne. The Hebrew daq means fine or small, used of the thin ears of corn; raq of the lean kine — both words for a thing that has no substance in it.
biblical_def: The word belongs to a dream and to the seven years it foretold. “And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them” (Gen 41:6); “And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears. And Pharaoh awoke, and, behold, it was a dream” (Gen 41:7). Pharaoh retells it to Joseph in the same terms — “seven ears, withered, thin, and blasted with the east wind” (Gen 41:23) — and adds that the magicians could not declare it (Gen 41:24). Joseph gives the interpretation without hesitation and without crediting himself: “And the seven thin and ill favoured kine that came up after them are seven years; and the seven empty ears blasted with the east wind shall be seven years of famine” (Gen 41:27). The detail that makes the dream terrible is that the thin devoured the full and were none the better for it — the famine would swallow the plenty and leave no trace of it, as verse thirty says, all the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt (Gen 41:30). Abundance does not survive itself; it must be stored under a word from God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thin as having little thickness or extent from one surface to the opposite; rare, not dense; lean, slim, small — and figuratively, not abundant.
webster_full: THIN, a. Having little thickness or extent from one surface to the opposite; as a thin plate of metal.
2. Rare; not dense; applied to fluids or to substances.
3. Not close; not crowded; not filling the space; as, the corn is thin.
4. Lean; slim; small; slender. Seven thin ears. Gen. xli.
scriptures: Gen 41:6
And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them.
Gen 41:7
And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears. And Pharaoh awoke, and, behold, it was a dream.
And the seven thin and ill favoured kine that came up after them are seven years; and the seven empty ears blasted with the east wind shall be seven years of famine.
And there shall arise after them seven years of famine; and all the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt; and the famine shall consume the land;
corruption_summary: Prosperity is assumed to be self-sustaining, though the dream says the thin years devour the full ones and leave no mark of what was eaten.
corruption_paragraphs: The strangest detail of Pharaoh's dream is not that the lean kine ate the fat, but what the king reports afterwards: when they had eaten them up, it could not be known that they had eaten them, but they were still ill favoured. The famine will consume seven years of surplus and look no better for it. That is a picture of every accumulation not held under God: it is spent, and the spending leaves no improvement behind. Joseph's counsel is therefore not to trust the plenty but to lay up under a word already given — a fifth part of the produce, in the cities, against years foretold. Faith and provision are not rivals here. It was the man who believed the dream came from God who told Egypt to build storehouses, and the man who did not believe would have eaten the seven years and been surprised.

The second thing is where the interpretation came from. The magicians of Egypt could not declare it; Joseph, brought hastily out of the dungeon and shaved, said to Pharaoh, It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace. He does not soften the message to keep his place, and he does not claim the gift. Both halves matter. Our own age has an appetite for men who can read the times — the forecasters, the analysts, the confident interpreters of what is coming — and the appetite is not new; Pharaoh had a whole guild of them. What Egypt actually needed was a Hebrew slave who would say plainly that the answer was God's and that seven bad years were coming. The thin ears devoured the full ones, and the only thing that survived was what had been stored on the strength of a word.
roots_summary: Hebrew daq (H1851), fine, thin, of the ears of corn; raq (H7534), lean, of the kine; with qadim (H6921), the east wind that blasted them.
roots_lines: Hebrew daq (H1851) — thin, fine, small; seven thin ears blasted with the east wind; Genesis 41:6.
Hebrew raq (H7534) — lean, thin; the seven thin and ill favoured kine; Genesis 41:27.
Hebrew qadim (H6921) — the east wind; the scorching sirocco that blasted the ears; Genesis 41:6, Hosea 13:15.
Hebrew raab (H7458) — famine; seven years of famine, and the plenty forgotten; Genesis 41:30.
Hebrew chalom (H2472) — a dream; doubled to Pharaoh because the thing was established by God; Genesis 41:32.
usage: “Seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind” — and they devoured the full.
“All the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt” — abundance does not survive itself.
“It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace” — the interpreter's first sentence.

pos: adj. (red-complexioned, healthy in colour; used of David twice, of the Nazarites, and of the Beloved in the Song)
etymology: Old English rudig, from rudu, redness, akin to red. The Hebrew admoni is from adom, red — the same root as Adam and as Edom.
biblical_def: The word attaches itself to David at both of his great introductions. At his anointing Samuel is told to look past appearance, and then the appearance is described anyway: he was ruddy, and withal of a beautiful countenance, and goodly to look to, and the LORD said, Arise, anoint him: for this is he. The lesson had been given a verse earlier: “man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1Sa 16:7). At the valley of Elah the same colour is used against him: “And when the Philistine looked about, and saw David, he disdained him: for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and of a fair countenance” (1Sa 17:42). What God did not choose him for, Goliath despised him for. Lamentations uses the word of Jerusalem's Nazarites before the ruin: “purer than snow… whiter than milk, they were more ruddy in body than rubies, their polishing was of sapphire” (Lam 4:7). And the Song gives it its highest use: “My beloved is white and ruddy, the chiefest among ten thousand” (Son 5:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ruddy as of a red color; of a lively flesh color, or the color of the human skin in high health; and, of things, red or reddish.
webster_full: RUDDY, a. Of a red color; of a lively flesh color, or the color of the human skin in high health.
Now he was ruddy, and withal of a beautiful countenance. 1 Sam. xvi.
2. Of a bright yellow color, as ruddy gold. [Improper.]
RUDDINESS, n. The state of being ruddy; redness or freshness of complexion.
scriptures: And when the Philistine looked about, and saw David, he disdained him: for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and of a fair countenance.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Son 5:10
My beloved is white and ruddy, the chiefest among ten thousand.
Lam 4:7
Her Nazarites were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk, they were more ruddy in body than rubies, their polishing was of sapphire:
corruption_summary: The Song of Solomon is either drained into pure allegory or reduced to an erotic anthology, when it is a real marriage song whose Beloved the church has always seen as pointing to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Two readings of the Song contend, and both lose something the book contains. The older allegorical excess made every detail a cipher and lost the plain sense: the Song is a marriage song, its love is bodily and honourable, and Scripture is not embarrassed by what God made and blessed in Eden before the fall. The modern reduction runs the other way, treating the book as ancient love poetry with no reference beyond itself, and it loses what the whole canon supplies — that marriage is from the beginning a figure of Christ and the church, which Paul states outright and calls a great mystery. The dictionary follows the Reformed line: the literal sense is real and good, and the typical sense is genuinely there because God appointed marriage to signify it. White and ruddy, the chiefest among ten thousand is said first of a bridegroom, and the church has never been wrong to hear in it the altogether lovely One.

David's ruddiness makes the other point, and it makes it twice. Samuel is warned not to judge by appearance, and God then chooses the handsome youngest son — which shows that the warning was not a rule against beauty but against reading the heart off the face. Then Goliath sees the same ruddy face and despises it, and is killed by the boy he despised. Appearance told Samuel nothing and told the Philistine something false. Our own moment is more governed by appearance than any before it, with faces sorted and ranked by machinery all day long, and the corruption is not that people notice beauty — Scripture notices it constantly, of Sarah, Rachel, Joseph, David and Absalom — but that appearance has become a verdict. The LORD looketh on the heart, and the passage says so in the same breath as it says the boy was good to look upon.
roots_summary: Hebrew admoni (H132), ruddy, red-haired or red-complexioned, from adom (H122), red; used of Esau at birth and twice of David.
roots_lines: Hebrew admoni (H132) — ruddy; used of Esau coming out red, and of David at his anointing and at Elah; Genesis 25:25, 1 Samuel 17:42.
Hebrew adom (H122) — red; my beloved is white and ruddy; Song of Solomon 5:10.
Hebrew tsach (H6703) — dazzling, white, clear; the first half of the Beloved's description; Song of Solomon 5:10.
Hebrew nazir (H5139) — one separated, a Nazarite; more ruddy in body than rubies before the siege; Lamentations 4:7.
Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart; what the LORD looks on while man looks on the eyes; 1 Samuel 16:7.
usage: “He was but a youth, and ruddy” — what Goliath despised him for.
“Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” — said just before the boy is described.
“My beloved is white and ruddy, the chiefest among ten thousand” — a bridegroom, and more.

pos: adj. (overgrown with mould; the state of the bread by which the Gibeonites deceived Joshua)
etymology: From mould, a growth on decaying matter, Middle English mowlde. The Hebrew niqqud here means crumbly or spotted — bread deliberately aged to tell a lie about distance.
biblical_def: Both occurrences are in one deception. The Gibeonites, hearing what had happened to Jericho and Ai, dressed a delegation to look as though it had come a very long way: “And old shoes and clouted upon their feet, and old garments upon them; and all the bread of their provision was dry and mouldy” (Jos 9:5). Then they said it in words: “This our bread we took hot for our provision out of our houses on the day we came forth to go unto you; but now, behold, it is dry, and it is mouldy” (Jos 9:12). The evidence was manufactured, and it worked, because Israel examined the evidence instead of asking God: the men took of their victuals and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD. “And Joshua made peace with them, and made a league with them, to let them live: and the princes of the congregation sware unto them” (Jos 9:15). Three days later the truth came out — “they heard that they were their neighbours, and that they dwelt among them” (Jos 9:16) — and the oath still stood. Israel kept it, and four centuries later God avenged Saul's breach of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mouldy as overgrown with mould; covered or filled with the minute fungous growth that appears on damp or decaying substances.
webster_full: MOULD, n. Concreted matter; a substance like down which forms on bodies which lie long in warm and damp air.
MOULDY, a. Overgrown with mould.
All the bread of their provision was dry and mouldy. Josh. ix.
MOULDINESS, n. The state of being mouldy.
scriptures: Jos 9:5
And old shoes and clouted upon their feet, and old garments upon them; and all the bread of their provision was dry and mouldy.
Jos 9:12
This our bread we took hot for our provision out of our houses on the day we came forth to go unto you; but now, behold, it is dry, and it is mouldy:
Jos 9:15
And Joshua made peace with them, and made a league with them, to let them live: and the princes of the congregation sware unto them.
Jos 9:16
And it came to pass at the end of three days after they had made a league with them, that they heard that they were their neighbours, and that they dwelt among them.
corruption_summary: Joshua 9 is the standing warning that examined evidence is not the same as sought counsel, and it is the step the chapter says Israel skipped.
corruption_paragraphs: Israel did not act carelessly by modern standards. They questioned the delegation, they inspected the provisions, they handled the cracked wineskins and the mouldy bread, and the physical evidence supported the story in every particular. The chapter's verdict on all this diligence is one clause: they asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD. That is the sentence to hang over every decision made by good process. Evidence can be manufactured; a document can be produced; references can be arranged; and a man who has checked everything checkable may still have consulted no one who knows what he cannot see. Prayer in Scripture is not a devotional garnish on a decision otherwise well made. It is the step by which a people who cannot see the heart ask the One who can.

The second half of the chapter is harder and more instructive. When the deception came out three days later, the congregation murmured against the princes and wanted the Gibeonites destroyed. The princes refused, on one ground: we have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel; now therefore we may not touch them. The oath had been obtained by fraud, and it still bound, because the name sworn by was God's and the honour at stake was His. Israel kept it. Centuries afterwards Saul, in his zeal, broke it and slew Gibeonites, and God sent a three-year famine in David's reign on that account. So the chapter that begins with a bad decision ends by teaching how a bad decision is to be handled: not by pretending it did not happen, and not by adding a broken word to a foolish one, but by keeping faith and bearing the cost.
roots_summary: Hebrew niqqud (H5350), crumbs or mouldy bread; with yabesh (H3001), dry, and shaba (H7650), to swear — the oath that outlived the fraud.
roots_lines: Hebrew niqqud (H5350) — crumbled, mouldy bread; used only in Joshua 9 and in a gift of cracknels; Joshua 9:5, 1 Kings 14:3.
Hebrew yabesh (H3001) — dry, withered; the bread was dry and mouldy; Joshua 9:12.
Hebrew shaba (H7650) — to swear; the princes of the congregation sware unto them; Joshua 9:15.
Hebrew shaal (H7592) — to ask, to enquire; they asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD; Joshua 9:14.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant, a league; made in error and kept for centuries; Joshua 9:15.
usage: “All the bread of their provision was dry and mouldy” — evidence manufactured for a lie.
“The princes of the congregation sware unto them” — and the oath outlived the fraud.
“They heard that they were their neighbours” — three days too late, and the word still held.
